title: The Toddler Language Explosion
hook: Somewhere in the second year, many toddlers go from a handful of words to picking up new ones almost daily — and talking with them is what fuels it.
key_points: Vocabulary often grows slowly at first, then accelerates rapidly during the second year.
Everyday talking, reading, and naming things builds language faster than screens do.
Understanding (what they grasp) usually runs ahead of speaking (what they can say).
Children vary a lot; persistent concerns about speech or hearing are worth a professional check.
content_html: Many parents notice a tipping point in the second year: a toddler who knew only a few words suddenly seems to add new ones every day. This "language explosion" is a normal pattern — vocabulary tends to build slowly at first and then accelerate as the pieces click into place.
extra_html: The biggest driver is plain old interaction. Talking through the day, reading together, naming objects, and responding to your child's attempts at words all do more for language than screen time does. It also helps to remember that understanding usually runs ahead of speaking — your toddler likely grasps far more than they can say yet. Children vary widely in timing, so resources like the CDC milestone lists are a guide rather than a scoreboard; persistent worries about speech or hearing are worth raising with a clinician. This is general educational information.

related.title: Why Toddlers Have Tantrums
related.hook: Tantrums are a normal part of toddler development — big feelings hitting a brain that can't yet manage them or fully put them into words.

related.title: Play Is How Young Children Learn
related.hook: For young children, play isn't a break from learning — it is the learning, building language, problem-solving, and social skills all at once.

related.title: How Language Unfolds — and When to Check
related.hook: Understanding always runs ahead of talking. Knowing the rough order of language milestones — and the handful of red flags — helps you tell normal variation from a delay worth acting on.

flashcards.prompt: What does the most to fuel a toddler's language growth?
flashcards.back_html: Everyday interaction — talking, reading, and naming things together. Back-and-forth conversation builds language far better than screens.

flashcards.prompt: How do a toddler's understanding and speaking abilities usually compare?

choices.text: Understanding typically runs ahead of speaking

flashcards.explanation_html: Toddlers usually comprehend far more than they can yet say. Receptive language (understanding) leads expressive language (speaking).
